title: Hinsdale County Wells: Depth, Yield & Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hinsdale County wells have an 86 ft median depth. Compare reported yields, $11,600-$20,600 finished-well costs, water levels and mountain-lot risks.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Hinsdale County
intro_html:
A relatively shallow county median does not make every Hinsdale County well a shallow job. Reported depths center on 86 feet, but fractured mountain bedrock can change the drilling outcome from one parcel to the next.

Colorado DWR records contain 1,257 well permits in the county, with 838 recorded as constructed. For land around Lake City or elsewhere in Hinsdale County, use these figures as a starting point, then check nearby completion records, access conditions and the permit’s allowed uses.

sections.heading: An 86-Foot Median, With Room for Much Deeper Drilling
sections.html:
Among the 816 wells reporting depth, the median is 86 feet and the middle half runs from 42 to 200 feet. That is a broad bidding range: a contractor should not price a parcel solely around the county median. The 90th-percentile depth is 382 feet, showing that substantially deeper work is part of the local record.

Permits mostly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. In granite and gneiss, usable water depends on intersecting connected fractures, not simply reaching a predictable layer. Compare nearby wells in similar terrain around Lake City, rather than substituting averages from San Juan County or Mineral County. Ask how additional footage, casing and difficult ground affect the bid.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Are Encouraging, but Test the Individual Well
sections.html:
The 305 wells with reported pump yields have a 15.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm. Those results are encouraging for household supply, but they describe reported tests—not a promise of sustained output at your lot.

In the reporting group, 2% produce under 1 gpm and 12% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. A low-output well can require storage and careful demand management. Before buying, request a pumping and recovery test rather than relying on the seller’s description. A strong pump rating does not establish aquifer capacity, and physical yield does not expand the uses allowed by the well permit.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Documented Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to standing water before pumping, not the total depth of the borehole. Only 69 wells report this measurement. Their median is 40 feet below ground, with the middle half from 19 to 75 feet.

The decade medians move from 88 feet below ground in the 2010s to 30 feet in the 2020s. The newer median is shallower, so this series does not show a dropping water table. It also does not establish countywide recovery: these records are not necessarily repeated measurements of the same wells. For a purchase, current static level, pumping drawdown and recovery at the actual well are more useful than that comparison alone.

sections.heading: Hinsdale’s Permit Activity Peaked in the 1990s
sections.html:
Recorded permit issuance increased from 138 in the 1970s to 230 in the 1980s, then reached 256 in the 1990s. The records list 194 in the 2000s, 111 in the 2010s and 68 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The latest decade is incomplete and should not be compared as a full decade.

Bob Williams Drilling Co. (Williams, Robert F.) leads the listed drillers with 341 records, followed by Irrigation Engineering & Supp. (Burk, Coy) with 57 and Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.) with 48. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Domestic/household use accounts for 78% of the permit use mix.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole in Mountain Bedrock
sections.html:
The supplied Hinsdale County cost model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 86-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $5,600–$8,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $11,600–$20,600.

Treat those figures as a planning allowance, not a parcel-specific quote. The 42–200-foot middle depth range alone gives a driller reason to spell out footage charges. Mountain access, rig setup, casing and grout requirements, and the route to the house also matter. Request a written scope showing what is included, what changes with depth, and what you owe if drilling does not find a usable supply.

sections.heading: Mine Features, Water Testing and Septic Placement
sections.html:
The environmental mapping lists 805 historic mine features, 4 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 4 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped features are reasons to investigate location and drainage—not evidence that a particular household well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location does not by itself establish a detection.

For an existing well, arrange laboratory testing for bacteria and nitrate, then discuss metals and other site-specific testing with the laboratory or local health authority. Inspect the wellhead, casing seal and drainage. Fractured rock can produce low yield or an unsuccessful hole, so review those contract terms too. Locate septic, the building footprint and well access together before committing to site work.

sections.heading: Before Closing on a Lake City or Hinsdale County Lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and completion report for the parcel, then compare neighboring wells with similar terrain and geology. The county’s 838 recorded constructed wells offer a useful starting point, but a permit entry alone does not prove an operable water supply. For an existing home, obtain current yield and water-quality results.

For vacant land, confirm permit eligibility and intended uses before finalizing the house and septic layout. An exempt household-use permit does not automatically allow outdoor irrigation or livestock watering. Uses outside an exemption may require an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin. Keep room for drilling equipment and future service access, and resolve the water-supply contingency before closing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hinsdale County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth is 86 feet, and the middle half ranges from 42 to 200 feet. These figures come from 816 depth reports. Fractured mountain bedrock makes individual results variable, so nearby completion records in similar terrain are a better bidding guide than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hinsdale County?
faq.a: The local planning model uses $65–$100 per foot. At the 86-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $5,600–$8,600, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $11,600–$20,600. Ask for a parcel-specific quote addressing access, casing, extra depth and unsuccessful drilling.

faq.q: How much water do Hinsdale County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yield has a 15.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm across 305 reports. However, 2% report under 1 gpm. Have the actual well tested for sustained pumping and recovery before buying; a recorded yield is not a guarantee of present performance.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Hinsdale County?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from permit records or proximity alone. Mapping lists 805 historic mine features, 4 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 4 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test the specific well for bacteria and nitrate, and ask a laboratory or health authority about metals and other site-specific concerns.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Hinsdale County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a decline: reported static water depth changes from 88 feet below ground in the 2010s to 30 feet in the 2020s. Only 69 wells report static levels, and the groups may contain different wells. This comparison cannot establish a countywide trend or predict conditions at your parcel.
